content: Hydrochlorothiazide is a thiazide diuretic approved by the FDA for the treatment of hypertension. It can be used as a standalone therapy or in combination with other antihypertensive agents. Common side effects include hypotension, phototoxicity, and vertigo. The recommended daily dose is 5 mg, and doses exceeding 50 mg per day are not advised. Off-label use of hydrochlorothiazide in adults is limited, with doses ranging from 5 to 25 mg per day. Pediatric use is also limited, with FDA-labeled indications and dosages not well established. Off-label pediatric dosing ranges from 5 to 2 mg/kg/day, with a typical dose of 1 mg/kg/day. Hydrochlorothiazide is contraindicated in patients with anuria or hypersensitivity to sulfonamide-derived drugs. It may cause acute myopia and secondary angle-closure glaucoma, which can lead to permanent vision loss if untreated. Symptoms such as decreased visual acuity or ocular pain typically occur within hours to weeks of starting the drug. Discontinuation of the drug is the primary treatment, and additional medical or surgical interventions may be necessary if intraocular pressure remains uncontrolled. Risk factors include a history of sulfonamide or penicillin allergy. In diabetic patients, latent diabetes mellitus may become apparent, and insulin dose adjustments may be required. Patients with impaired renal function may experience cumulative effects of the drug, potentially leading to azotemia. Periodic monitoring of serum electrolytes is recommended to detect imbalances such as hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hypochloremic alkalosis, and hypomagnesemia. Warning signs of fluid and electrolyte imbalance include dry mouth, thirst, weakness, lethargy, drowsiness, restlessness, muscle pain or cramps, muscular fatigue, hypotension, oliguria, tachycardia, and gastrointestinal disturbances like nausea and vomiting. Hypokalemia is more likely to occur with brisk diuresis, severe cirrhosis, prolonged therapy, or concurrent use of corticosteroids or ACTH. It can also result from inadequate oral electrolyte intake. Hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia may provoke ventricular arrhythmias or exacerbate the toxic effects of digitalis on the heart. Potassium supplementation or increased intake of potassium-rich foods can help prevent or treat hypokalemia. Dilutional hyponatremia, which can be life-threatening, may occur in edematous patients during hot weather. Water restriction is the preferred treatment, except in rare cases of life-threatening hyponatremia, where salt administration may be necessary. In cases of actual salt depletion, appropriate replacement therapy is recommended. Hyperuricemia or acute gout may be precipitated in some patients receiving thiazide diuretics. Caution is advised in patients with impaired hepatic function, as thiazides can precipitate hepatic coma in those with severe liver disease. Thiazides decrease calcium excretion and may cause hypercalcemia and hypophosphatemia, leading to parathyroid gland changes in some patients on prolonged therapy. Adverse reactions include weakness, hypotension (including orthostatic hypotension), vertigo, paresthesia, dizziness, headache, restlessness, aplastic anemia, agranulocytosis, leukopenia, hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, pancreatitis, jaundice, diarrhea, vomiting, sialadenitis, cramping, constipation, gastric irritation, nausea, anorexia, anaphylactic reactions, necrotizing angiitis, respiratory distress, photosensitivity, fever, urticaria, rash, purpura, electrolyte imbalance, hyperglycemia, glycosuria, hyperuricemia, muscle spasm, renal failure, interstitial nephritis, erythema multiforme, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, exfoliative dermatitis, alopecia, blurred vision, xanthopsia, and impotence. Drug interactions include potentiation of orthostatic hypotension with alcohol, barbiturates, or narcotics. Dosage adjustments of antidiabetic drugs may be required. Additive effects or potentiation may occur with other antihypertensive drugs. Cholestyramine and colestipol resins reduce hydrochlorothiazide absorption. Corticosteroids and ACTH may intensify electrolyte depletion, particularly hypokalemia. Lithium clearance is reduced by diuretics, increasing the risk of lithium toxicity. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) may reduce the diuretic, natriuretic, and antihypertensive effects of hydrochlorothiazide. Hydrochlorothiazide is classified as Pregnancy Category B by the FDA. Animal studies have shown no evidence of harm to the fetus, but adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women are lacking. Thiazides cross the placental barrier and may cause fetal or neonatal jaundice, thrombocytopenia, and other adverse reactions observed in adults. Use during pregnancy should be limited to cases where it is clearly needed. Thiazides are excreted in breast milk, and a decision should be made to discontinue nursing or the drug, considering its importance to the mother. Hydrochlorothiazide is well absorbed following oral administration, with bioavailability ranging from 65% to 75%. Absorption is reduced in patients with congestive heart failure. The drug is primarily eliminated via renal pathways, with 55% to 77% of the administered dose excreted unchanged in urine. Plasma concentrations are increased, and the elimination half-life is prolonged in patients with renal disease. The mechanism of action involves blocking sodium and chloride reabsorption in the distal tubule, increasing sodium and water excretion. This can lead to compensatory mechanisms that may cause excessive loss of potassium, hydrogen, and chloride ions. The drug also decreases calcium and uric acid excretion, may increase iodide excretion, and may reduce glomerular filtration rate. Acute antihypertensive effects are thought to result from reduced blood volume and cardiac output, while chronic effects involve decreased peripheral vascular resistance. The exact mechanism of its antihypertensive effect is unknown. Hydrochlorothiazide is available in 5 mg capsules for oral use. Inactive ingredients include colloidal silicon dioxide, corn starch, lactose monohydrate, and magnesium stearate. Capsules contain gelatin and various colorants. Storage conditions require protection from light, moisture, and freezing, with a recommended temperature range of 20°-25°C (68°-77°F).
